edges.relationship: Cronon criticizes Turner’s vague frontier categories and 1890 closure, replacing homogeneous frontier stages with differentiated regional connections (1987).
edges.evidence_note: Selected printed 158–167,174–176. The account of previous critics is distinguished from Cronon’s own regional alternative. Criticism is not wholesale rejection: he retains Turner’s interdisciplinary questions;165n 28 expressly distinguishes writing from teaching.

edges.relationship: Turner remains an explicitly acknowledged organizing foil for Cronon’s teaching and questions about regional environments, despite Cronon’s criticism (1987).
edges.evidence_note: 160n 14 describes Cronon’s own course organization;175–176 recovers continuing questions. An acknowledged critical resource, not endorsement of the frontier thesis or a teacher–student relationship.

edges.relationship: White reads Turner’s settlement story alongside Buffalo Bill’s conquest story as complementary frontier myths that marginalize Indigenous dispossession (1994).
edges.evidence_note: Selected White transcription corroborated by Richard W. Steele’s complete 1995 scholarly review. Exact book pagination and illustrations uncollated; the full chapter remains unread. This is White’s interpretation of Turner, not independent validation of every exhibition object.

edges.relationship: Hofstadter criticizes Turner’s weak critical response to expansion, Indigenous dispossession and anti-Mexican and anti-Chinese nativism, as quoted by Bogue (1994).
edges.evidence_note: Bogue 206 and 220n 38 visually checked. His quotation identifies The Progressive Historians,104,106 in a 1969 manifestation. Hofstadter’s original chapter and 1949 essay remain unread; the claim is expressly mediated by Bogue.

edges.relationship: Deloria criticizes Turner’s frontier boundary for naturalizing Indigenous difference and an expectation of inevitable white triumph (2002).
edges.evidence_note: Primary publisher excerpt 8–10, with 6–7 framing. Deloria situates Turner within a longer frontier paradigm; this neither makes Turner its sole inventor nor treats all Indigenous historiography as one position. Remaining chapter unread.

edges.relationship: Taylor criticizes the continued use of Turner’s racial and national types in Kluger’s expansion narrative, arguing for differentiated Indigenous and colonial histories (2008).
edges.evidence_note: Own scholarly review paragraphs on Turner and Kluger, especially “Like Turner, Kluger insists” and the French-war comparison. The immediate object is Kluger’s recycled Turner; his attributed Limerick quotation is not assigned to Taylor as original wording. Book unread.

edges.relationship: Wolfe explicitly agrees that frontier closure marks a major change, interpreting the post-frontier shift through Indigenous containment and assimilation within continuing settler colonialism (2013).
edges.evidence_note: Primary 257–259, especially 258, and 276 n 19. Qualified agreement is not blanket defense or proved influence. This remains an undirected comparison/reception link; Native sovereignty and continuing elimination remain central to Wolfe’s different account.

edges.relationship: Foner explicitly identifies Black Reconstruction and Du Bois’s account of the Civil War as resources for his interpretation of emancipation and revolution.
edges.evidence_note: Foner’s own 2015 answers recount using Black Reconstruction and expressly identify his agreement with Du Bois. This is a bounded acknowledgment, not proof of every influence on Foner or a claim that his family acquaintance alone establishes intellectual transmission.

edges.relationship: Noiriel explicitly acknowledges Bourdieu’s sociology as an influence on the collective development of socio-history while declining school allegiance.
edges.evidence_note: First 2012 answer. The collective is described by Noiriel as including his own generation and practice; no formal master–disciple relation or adoption of all Bourdieu’s positions is asserted.

edges.relationship: Noiriel criticizes Bourdieu’s later public interventions for presenting political judgments with the undifferentiated authority of researched scholarship.
edges.evidence_note: Second 2012 answer on fundamental research and essays, explicitly naming Raisons d’Agir interventions. This is Noiriel’s critique of the distinction between expertise and public intervention, not a rejection of all Bourdieu’s sociology.

edges.relationship: Noiriel explicitly uses Wittgenstein’s game and language-game metaphor to explain socio-history as shared rules of practice rather than an all-purpose theory.
edges.evidence_note: First 2012 answer, paragraph beginning “La socio-histoire, ce n’est pas une théorie.” A named methodological metaphor, not blanket adoption of Wittgenstein’s philosophy.

edges.relationship: Tilly contests Vernon’s linguistic explanation and subjectivist definition of democracy, arguing that Vernon’s own evidence also supports a modest expansion of democratic control (1994).
edges.evidence_note: Selected journal review 260–262 and 265–268 opening. Tilly also praises Vernon’s empirical richness and raises competing criteria, not an independently settled verdict. Mixed edge_1161 remains because it includes other readers and later works.

edges.relationship: Tilly criticizes Joyce’s treatment of class and language for obscuring relational agency and causal explanation, while valuing the empirical research (1994).
edges.evidence_note: Selected review 260–265. Tilly’s account is attributed; the underlying book is not independently adjudicated here. The mixed debate summary and its other named critics remain intact.

edges.relationship: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and a sharp individual/collective resistance opposition (2001), then specifies objections about revolutionary aspiration, coercive force and resistance in “On Agency” (2003), without saying Genovese ignored enslaved agency.
edges.evidence_note: Two separately dated primary interventions consolidated as one relationship. 2001 scholarly rereading: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and the sharp opposition between individual resistance and collective revolt, while affirming the book’s lasting value (2001). Complete scholarly rereading. Johnson argues for coerced rule and a continuum of resistance; he explicitly rejects the simplistic charge that Genovese denied enslaved people agency. Original historical examples and Roll, Jordan, Roll remain uncollated. Reading extent: Fresh complete review read through the final day-to-day resistance paragraph. Distinguishes Genovese’s hegemony argument from denying enslaved agency; criticizes paternalism, coerced rule and a strict individual/collective resistance opposition while affirming the book’s value. The original book and historical examples are not independently audited. 2003 “On Agency”: Johnson rejects three premises of Genovese’s resistance/hegemony account while rejecting the claim that Roll, Jordan, Roll simply ignores enslaved agency (2003). The named p. 117 criticism concerns revolutionary aspiration, culture versus coercive force, and the individual/collective distinction. It is not a denial that Genovese discussed resistance. Reading extent: Fresh primary pp113–114,117 and122–123 read; Genovese’s books were not newly read. These are not a single publication or a second independent edge. The original Genovese book and underlying historical examples are not independently collated.

edges.relationship: Genovese adapts Gramscian hegemony to explain how paternalist relations could mediate slaveholding class rule, as Walter Johnson explicates (2001).
edges.evidence_note: Johnson’s own substantive account distinguishes Genovese’s use of hegemony from denying agency and then criticizes its application. Named-reader mediation is explicit; no certification of Genovese’s full book or Gramsci originals. The existing mixed Genovese/Gutman edge_162 stays.

edges.relationship: McGirr explicitly credits Cohen’s Chicago research while placing greater weight on Prohibition and the election of 1928 in the formation of cross-ethnic political loyalties (2016).
edges.evidence_note: McGirr’s own answer to the Making a New Deal question. She calls the emphases distinct but not incompatible; this is an acknowledged debt and extension, not a claim that she repudiates Cohen or derives all her work from her.

edges.relationship: McGirr explicitly agrees with Gerstle’s account of the American state as unevenly powerful, connecting public/private authority and federal tensions to Prohibition (2016).
edges.evidence_note: Own answer on the weak-state myth names both Gerstle and Novak. This link records her specific agreement with Gerstle’s formulation; Novak is not merged into him. Agreement alone does not prove transmission, so the link stays undirected.

edges.relationship: Carter’s appreciative review of On the Edge of Empire asks for fuller North American comparison and more evidence of Indigenous social centrality, political agency and initiatives (2002/03).
edges.evidence_note: The signed review praises the gender/race analysis and conclusion while making these two requests on p. 119. It does not say Perry denied Indigenous resistance. The reviewed book is not newly read.

edges.relationship: With Linda Kealey, Iacovetta answers Sangster’s Beyond Dichotomies, objecting that its polemic risks oversimplification and misrepresentation while welcoming debate (1996).
edges.evidence_note: The opening expressly names Sangster’s essay and frames the response as disagreement among friends and colleagues. Linda Kealey is coauthor; she is not Gregory S.Kealey. Do not treat this as a single-author reply.

edges.relationship: Replying to Iacovetta and Linda Kealey, Sangster welcomes their review but contests the simplification charge and treats gender as both standpoint and field (1996).
edges.evidence_note: This is a qualified rejoinder: p. 247 stresses shared questions and theoretical overlap. It must not turn Iacovetta/Kealey into simple poststructuralist adversaries or erase the coauthor.

edges.relationship: Sangster questions Valverde’s suggestion that women’s history is not self-sufficient, reading it as implying gender history’s superiority (1996).
edges.evidence_note: The attribution is explicit in p. 240 n3; this records Sangster’s reading, not an agreed hierarchy.

edges.relationship: Sangster objects that Parr groups feminist and antifeminist critics of gender history together (1996).
edges.evidence_note: The criticism is confined to p. 240 n2 and its quoted passage; it does not reject Parr’s entire gender-history project.

edges.relationship: Sangster contrasts Canadian feminist materialist work with what she calls Scott’s more radical antimaterialist deconstruction (2000).
edges.evidence_note: The wording is Sangster’s characterization. Her neighbouring objection about constructed materiality targets Sewell, not Scott.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Reasoning Otherwise, Palmer challenges McKay’s elastic liberal-order category for obscuring capitalism’s changing structures while praising the book’s achievement (2009).
edges.evidence_note: The review names McKay and the 2008 book. This adds personal visibility to the existing field critique; it is not new evidence of a different dispute. No direct McKay rejoinder is established.

edges.relationship: Greer’s Sorel case challenges the demographic-and-cultural explanation of agrarian crisis associated with Ouellet, especially the routine-bound habitant premise (1981).
edges.evidence_note: The named work is identified in n41. This isolates Greer’s intervention without replacing the multi-author controversy or treating his unread 1993 book as direct evidence.

edges.relationship: Higginbotham explicitly uses Scott’s infrapolitics for her discussion of micropolitical resistance (1992).
edges.evidence_note: Her note67 identifies Domination and the Arts of Resistance, pp183–192; James C.Scott is distinct from Joan W.Scott.

edges.relationship: Higginbotham credits Hine’s reading, suggestions and questions on an earlier version of her 1992 article.
edges.evidence_note: This is a named draft-feedback contribution, not evidence that Hine originated the article’s theory.

edges.relationship: Higginbotham adapts Foucault’s technologies terminology to race, gender and sexuality (1992).
edges.evidence_note: Her p. 252 n4 names History of Sexuality1 and explains the term alongside Teresa de Lauretis; neither resource is exclusive.

edges.relationship: Roediger identifies Black Reconstruction as an intellectual entry point for connecting emancipation with broader labour freedom (acknowledged 2012).
edges.evidence_note: The written union interview directly records Roediger’s acknowledgment, not merely its interviewer’s introduction. It does not explain his whole research programme.

edges.relationship: Johnson explicitly uses Marx’s Eighteenth Brumaire formulation as an alternative starting point for rethinking agency (2003).
edges.evidence_note: The opening counterposes Marx’s constrained history-making formulation to Gutman’s Sartre-derived injunction; no universal Marxist lineage is inferred.

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty explicitly uses Bhabha’s pedagogic/performative distinction to formulate a tension within nationalism and peasant citizenship (2000).
edges.evidence_note: The acknowledgment is on p. 10. It concerns this conceptual distinction, not derivation of the whole provincializing-Europe project.

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty credits Foucault with encouraging critiques of historicism while explicitly denying that postcolonial criticism simply derives from Western poststructuralism (2000).
edges.evidence_note: Both the acknowledgment and the qualification occur together on p6. This must not become a one-way European-origin account.

edges.relationship: De Certeau praises Bourdieu’s descriptions of practical ingenuity but questions whether habitus and structural reproduction suppress the tactical inventiveness they reveal.
edges.evidence_note: Chapter IV, selected English pp. 50, 55–57, 59–60. This is de Certeau’s critical reading, including admiration for the descriptions, not a settled verdict on all Bourdieu. Complete books and original French remain unread for this audit.

edges.relationship: With Frederick Cooper, Brubaker questions Hall’s claim that identity remains analytically indispensable and proposes more differentiated terms for identification and group formation.
edges.evidence_note: Beyond Identity, pp. 8–9. The jointly authored criticism explicitly recognizes Hall’s sophisticated anti-essentialism; it does not characterize him as a simple essentialist or deny the political legitimacy of identity claims. Cooper retains equal authorship. One joint argument is projected here, not two independent studies. Joint-credit scope: the Brubaker-source and Cooper-source records project the same 2000 joint paper and the same target-specific argument; they are not independent studies or separate debate events. Both coauthors retain equal credit.

edges.relationship: With Frederick Cooper, Brubaker argues that Omi and Winant’s sharp ethnic/racial-group distinction insufficiently accommodates historical racialization of European immigrants and subsequent changes in racial categories.
edges.evidence_note: Beyond Identity, p. 40 note 28, specifically discussing Omi and Winant’s 1994 formulation. The authors acknowledge its constructivist definition but challenge this distinction; the edge is not a verdict on every racial-formation historian. Their cited historical studies were not independently reread. Cooper retains equal authorship. Joint-credit scope: the Brubaker-source and Cooper-source records project the same 2000 joint paper and the same target-specific argument; they are not independent studies or separate debate events. Both coauthors retain equal credit.

edges.relationship: Arendt challenges Marx’s elevation of labor and conflation of labor with work, identifying a tension between labor as distinctively human and emancipation from necessity.
edges.evidence_note: The Human Condition, selected pp. 79, 85–86, 88, 101–104 in the 1998 second edition. The argument dates to 1958. Arendt’s respect for Marx and recognition of labor-power analysis qualify this particular criticism; cited Marx originals were not independently collated.

edges.relationship: Butler argues that Foucault’s presentation of Herculine Barbin romanticizes pleasures outside power, conflicting with his own account of sexuality’s historical production.
edges.evidence_note: Gender Trouble, chapter III ii, 1999-edition pp. 119–120, 122–126. This is a specific immanent criticism alongside productive use of Foucault, not rejection of his entire project. Barbin’s memoir and Foucault originals were not newly read; this edition’s pagination is not silently assigned to the 1990 original.

edges.relationship: Ginzburg questions Foucault’s privileging of exclusion over excluded people, arguing that hostile or distorted records can still support inquiry into subordinate culture.
edges.evidence_note: The Cheese and the Worms, preface to the Italian edition, pp. xvii–xix in the English translation. Ginzburg credits the attention to exclusion before criticizing the Pierre Riviere collection’s refusal of interpretation. This is his attributed reading; the French originals and collection were not independently collated. John and Anne Tedeschi share translation credit.

edges.relationship: Agamben proposes to correct or complete Foucault’s biopolitics by placing bare life’s sovereign exclusion in an older political structure and treating its generalized exception as distinctive of modernity.
edges.evidence_note: Homo Sacer introduction, reformatted English digital pp. 10–13, especially p. 12. This is a theoretical corrective, not a proven universal historical sequence. The author explicitly disavows flattening the historical differences between democracy and totalitarianism. This differs from the existing Foucault-to-Agamben methodological resource. Stanford print pagination and full originals were not collated.

edges.relationship: Adorno questions Benjamin’s weighting of autonomous and technologically reproduced art, arguing that both contain domination and possibilities of change rather than assigning emancipation to mass reception alone.
edges.evidence_note: Letter of 18 March 1936, selected English collection pp. 120–124. Adorno acknowledges their common materialist aims and Benjamin’s contribution while criticizing this weighting. Letter date is not the English collection publication date. The complete correspondence, Benjamin essay and following 1938 letter were not newly collated.

edges.relationship: Spivak questions Deleuze’s account of oppressed subjects speaking transparently for themselves, insisting that representation and the international division of labour cannot be bypassed.
edges.evidence_note: Can the Subaltern Speak?, fresh abridged teaching excerpt pp. 24–25 and 27, alongside the preserved fuller 1993-reprint reading in the source record. The target is his position in the conversation with Foucault, not every Deleuze/Guattari work. Preserve the existing Foucault response; the two named interlocutors are not interchangeable.

edges.relationship: Pratt uses Anderson’s account of imagined communities to question homogeneous models of speech communities and distinguish them from unequal contact zones.
edges.evidence_note: Arts of the Contact Zone, Contact and Community, selected digital pp. 4–5 of the reformatted reproduction (not original journal page numbers). This is explicit analytical appropriation. Pratt does not claim Anderson believes real nations homogeneous, and this is not a reverse critique of Anderson. Broken reproduction footnote is not used as evidence.

edges.relationship: Gilroy identifies Du Bois’s double consciousness as a central organizing resource for his inquiry into the Black Atlantic.
edges.evidence_note: The Black Atlantic, preface p. x, visually checked after OCR reading of ix–xi. This is Gilroy’s explicit acknowledgment, not an inference from a subtitle. Chapter 4 and the Du Bois originals were not reread; the book’s provisional, anti-closure framework and scant treatment of Fanon and James remain qualified.

edges.relationship: Bloch’s dedication credits Febvre with ideas developed through their shared historical work and discussions (written 1941; published 1949).
edges.evidence_note: Apologie dedication, digital PDF p. 5, dated 10 May 1941. Bloch explicitly acknowledges ideas from Febvre while saying other ideas cannot be assigned to only one of them. This is his testimony about this methodological work, not proof that every Bloch argument derives from Febvre.

edges.relationship: Bloch credits the Durkheimian school with deeper analysis and more exacting historical questions while qualifying its earlier programme (Apologie).
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, digital PDF pp. 11–12, original introduction XV–XVI. The acknowledged resource is the sociological school as Bloch describes it; this does not substitute Émile Durkheim personally for Simiand or make all Bloch’s methods sociological. His gratitude coexists with criticism of rigid scientific laws.

edges.relationship: Bloch questions the early Durkheimian school’s rigid scientific ideal and its exclusion of events and individual life from rational knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Introduction, digital PDF pp. 11–12. Bloch also acknowledges later flexibility and explicitly expresses gratitude and respect. The target is the school’s earlier programme in his account, not a rejection of all sociology or all Durkheim’s work.

edges.relationship: Marc Verdure identifies Bloch as a methodological precedent for Duby’s 1970 programme of medieval social inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Collège de France institutional account, paragraph beginning with Duby’s 4 December 1970 inaugural lecture, read. This is Verdure’s situated methodological lineage, not evidence of personal supervision, exclusive school allegiance or a fresh reading of the original lecture.

edges.relationship: Marc Verdure identifies Febvre as a methodological precedent for Duby’s 1970 programme of medieval social inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Collège de France institutional account, paragraph beginning with Duby’s 4 December 1970 inaugural lecture, read. This is Verdure’s situated methodological lineage, not evidence of personal supervision, exclusive school allegiance or a fresh reading of the original lecture.

edges.relationship: Levi explicitly endorses Bourdieu’s warning against the biographical illusion of a coherent life and uses it within a plural approach to historical biography (1989).
edges.evidence_note: Les usages de la biographie, p. 1326, official primary OCR. Levi credits the criticism and the need to reconstruct social contexts; this is a particular conceptual use, not agreement with every Bourdieu position or a claim that Levi rejects biography.

edges.relationship: Nora expressly invokes Halbwachs’s account of group-specific, plural memories while distinguishing memory from historical reconstruction (1989 English translation).
edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 9, first paragraph, read in Marc Roudebush’s translation, alongside pp. 7–8. Nora’s memory/history opposition and civilizational language remain his historically situated formulation; the original French and Halbwachs’s full works are not newly collated.

edges.relationship: Careless explicitly credits Cook’s phrase and initial idea in explaining his own limited-identities programme.
edges.evidence_note: Limited Identities—Ten Years Later, opening and footnote 1. This is Careless’s own retrospective acknowledgement; he also disclaims paternity for the entire subsequent historiography. The 1969 article is not newly read, and the 1979 delivery/1980–81 issue-date qualifications remain.

edges.relationship: Skinner explicitly uses Kuhn’s priority-of-paradigms discussion in framing anachronistic interpretation in the history of ideas (1969).
edges.evidence_note: Meaning and Understanding, printed p. 7 and note 18, directly cites Structure, chapterV. Gombrich is a separately credited resource; Kuhn is not made the founder of Skinner’s method or the entire Cambridge grouping. Mixed Skinner/Dunn edge 617 remains unchanged; Ryle’s use by Dunn in 618 is not reassigned to Skinner.

edges.relationship: Darnton credits Geertz and their long-running anthropology/history seminar as resources for his anthropological historical practice.
edges.evidence_note: Darnton’s own 2018 interview answer 52, indexed primary text, describes a 20-year seminar and specifically connects this to The Great Cat Massacre. It is his retrospective acknowledgement, not proof of agreement on every interpretation, formal doctoral supervision or a freshly read complete book.

edges.relationship: Winters distinguishes digital history from archived-web inquiry while documenting their methodological overlap and growing exchange (2018).
edges.evidence_note: Repository manuscript pp. 4–6: discussion of digital history’s varied methods, limited earlier uptake of web archives and emerging cross-sector networks. This is her situated 2018 assessment, not a current census, a field-founding lineage or an equivalence between the two fields. Final book pagination is not used.

edges.relationship: Scott explicitly takes de Certeau’s incommensurability as a theoretical resource for a critical relationship between psychoanalysis and history (2012).
edges.evidence_note: The author’s abstract expressly names de Certeau’s theoretical contribution and distinguishes it from Lyndal Roper’s demonstration of limits and value. Abstract read through PubMed PMID 22413176; the article body and de Certeau’s complete works are not newly read.

edges.relationship: Ginzburg criticizes Derrida’s objections to Foucault’s historical standpoint as a nihilistic obstacle to inquiry into excluded people.
edges.evidence_note: This is Ginzburg’s attributed reading of Derrida. His suggestion that Derrida helped produce Foucault’s change of method is expressly tentative and is not made into a separate influence arrow. Derrida’s and Foucault’s originals were not newly read.

edges.relationship: Ginzburg disputes Furet’s restriction of subordinate-class history to quantitative and anonymous reconstruction, defending individual cases where the evidence permits.
edges.evidence_note: He explicitly names Furet before defending the possibility of reconstructing individual personalities. This is a methodological criticism, not rejection of quantitative history as such or proof of every Menocchio interpretation. Furet’s underlying text was not newly read.

edges.relationship: With Rogers Brubaker, Cooper questions Hall’s claim that identity is analytically indispensable and proposes more differentiated terms for identification and group formation.
edges.evidence_note: The joint paper recognizes Hall’s sophisticated anti-essentialism; it neither labels him a simple essentialist nor denies the political legitimacy of identity claims. This credits Cooper as an equal coauthor of the same jointly published criticism represented by the parallel Brubaker-source proposal; it does not assert an independent endorsement, second study or separate debate event. Joint-credit scope: the Brubaker-source and Cooper-source records project the same 2000 joint paper and the same target-specific argument; they are not independent studies or separate debate events. Both coauthors retain equal credit.

edges.relationship: With Rogers Brubaker, Cooper questions Omi and Winant’s sharp ethnic/racial-group distinction for inadequately accommodating European immigrants’ historical racialization and later categorical change.
edges.evidence_note: The joint paper acknowledges Omi and Winant’s constructivist definition before criticizing this specific distinction; it is not a verdict on every racial-formation historian. The historical studies cited in the note were not independently reread. This credits Cooper as an equal coauthor of the same jointly published criticism represented by the parallel Brubaker-source proposal; it does not assert an independent endorsement, second study or separate debate event. Joint-credit scope: the Brubaker-source and Cooper-source records project the same 2000 joint paper and the same target-specific argument; they are not independent studies or separate debate events. Both coauthors retain equal credit.

edges.relationship: Ginzburg cites Davis’s charivari research as an exemplary use of indirect evidence for popular culture.
edges.evidence_note: Preface to the Italian edition, English translation p. xvii. This records an explicitly praised methodological example in Ginzburg’s own argument. It does not claim that the cited scholar founded his practice, supplied the entire book’s method or endorsed Ginzburg. John and Anne Tedeschi’s translation and the 1976/1980/1992 distinction remain; the cited scholars’ complete works are not newly read.

edges.relationship: Ginzburg cites Thompson’s charivari research as an exemplary use of indirect evidence for popular culture.
edges.evidence_note: Preface to the Italian edition, English translation p. xvii. This records an explicitly praised methodological example in Ginzburg’s own argument. It does not claim that the cited scholar founded his practice, supplied the entire book’s method or endorsed Ginzburg. John and Anne Tedeschi’s translation and the 1976/1980/1992 distinction remain; the cited scholars’ complete works are not newly read.

edges.relationship: Ginzburg identifies Le Goff’s specification of cultural interaction as a productive example within his account of popular culture.
edges.evidence_note: Preface to the Italian edition, English translation p. xix. This records an explicitly praised methodological example in Ginzburg’s own argument. It does not claim that the cited scholar founded his practice, supplied the entire book’s method or endorsed Ginzburg. John and Anne Tedeschi’s translation and the 1976/1980/1992 distinction remain; the cited scholars’ complete works are not newly read.

sources.title: Theodor W. Adorno, letter to Walter Benjamin, 18 March 1936, English collection Aesthetics and Politics, selected pp. 120–124.

verification.note: Selected primary letter pages 120–124 read by OCR of rotated scanned spreads; heading establishes the letter date. The 1936 intervention is distinct from its later English collection. No sole translator credit is inferred from the collection editor. Adorno acknowledges a shared materialist project and potential in both autonomous and mass art. Complete correspondence, following 1938 letter and Benjamin’s original essay were not newly collated.

sources.title: Giorgio Agamben, Homo Sacer: Sovereign Power and Bare Life, translated by Daniel Heller-Roazen (English 1998; Italian original 1995), introduction.

verification.note: Selected primary introduction in reformatted English reproduction, digital/retyped pp. 10–13, read; especially the explicit proposal to correct or complete Foucault’s biopolitics. These are reproduction locators, not collated Stanford print page numbers. English credit/date corroborated by Indiana University catalogue https://iucat.iu.edu/iuc/1210603 . The text expressly does not flatten historical differences between democracy and totalitarianism. This is Agamben’s theoretical proposal, not an established universal history. Complete book, Italian original and Foucault originals not newly read.

verification.note: Selected primary printed pp. 79, 85–86, 88 and 101–104 read; second-edition imprint checked. The argument is from 1958, not a new 1998 intervention. Arendt respects Marx’s intellectual achievement and acknowledges labor-power analysis while criticizing the labor/work and emancipation formulation. Complete book and cited Marx originals not independently collated.

sources.title: Judith Butler, Gender Trouble (1990), 1999 Routledge edition, chapter III section ii.

These page locators belong to the 1999 edition, not a collated 1990 printing. Butler’s productive use of Foucault is retained alongside this specific criticism. Complete book, original Barbin memoir and Foucault originals were not newly reread.

Ginzburg credits attention to exclusions while criticizing the treatment of excluded people and refusal of interpretation. The original Italian, French Foucault works and Pierre Riviere collection were not independently read for this audit; this is Ginzburg’s attributed interpretation. Additional independently checked primary coverage, 2026-10-25: printed xviii–xx visually read for the Derrida/Furet responses; the coordinator also checked the examples/praise paragraphs on xvii and xix for Davis, Thompson and Le Goff. The 1976 Italian preface, 1980 joint Tedeschi English translation and 1992 paperback manifestation remain distinct. The cited scholars’ underlying works were not newly read; neither a whole-book reading nor a general formative debt is inferred.

edge_466.evidence_note: Cannadine’s 1990 review is the specified critical source. It records disagreement over connections to women’s rights and republicanism, not unanimous judgment or endorsement of the reviewer’s incidental biographical claims.

edge_1137.evidence_note: Judt (NYRB, 25 May 1995, read in full): the book's "defect, for there is really only one" is that "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; the claim that Sovietisation followed American intervention "is simply wrong"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject"; Hobsbawm "mostly avoids military or political narrative". Qualifications kept: Judt calls the book "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account", praises its economic analysis and calls The Age of Capital "Hobsbawm’s single greatest work". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.

edge_454.evidence_note: Primary p. 1512 uses The Cheese and the Worms when rejecting an automatic elite-text/popular-text division. The claim is limited to Ginzburg’s specific resource; not every member of the microhistory/everyday-life group is implicated.

rationale: Existing entries only. Named arguments, collaborator credit, original/translated/reprint dates and selected-reading limits remain explicit. One Johnson–Genovese relationship preserves distinct 2001 and 2003 interventions. Four Brubaker/Cooper records project two shared target-specific arguments, not four events. Old collective contexts remain, except 27 precisely guarded person routes and only three obsolete-availability clauses. Degree and this semantic screen do not prove an exhaustive intellectual network.
